This review of the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti graphics card benchmarks the performance of the new GPU, particularly with the 5070 Ti vs. the 5080, 4080 Super, 4070 Ti Super, AMD RX 7900 XTX, and similar cards. Benchmarking includes gaming performance tests of the best video cards in 2025, some revisits of older cards like the RTX 3070 and GTX 1070, and power consumption and efficiency tests. The GPU market is in an era of absurdity now, reminiscent of 2020. Price means nothing.

If you could find one, it was well over $1500-1800!!!!   We see the same bull over and over.   I'm guess the 5080 Super will be also well over 1500! if not, 2k!  Via the fact people are paying 2800-3000 for a 5090 shows NVIDIA there is NO limits to what they can get away with! comments.text:
The info regarding price and availability has shifted a lot since this video was created. If you already have a 4000 series GPU, it still remains true that it kind of doesn't make sense to upgrade. But for those on older generations, the 5070 TI is now sort of the sweetspot for Nvidia cards due to current pricing and availability. All the 4000 series cards being compared in this video against the 5070 TI are insanely overpriced compared to the 5070 ti. At time of writing this, I'm seeing a 300-500 dollar difference for 4070 ti super compared to the 5070 ti and that is not even discussing how its impossible to find a 4070 ti super for sale to begin with. From a price perspective, the cost per performance difference between the 5070 ti and 5080 doesn't justify paying more for a 5080. So the 5070 TI ends up being the better, more "affordable" Nvidia card moving into June 2025.

AMD is obviously an option, but if you look at markup above MSRP, their price points are equal to the 5070 ti. So you're technically paying more for AMD right now, compared to Nividia based on MSRP. Going with older gen AMD cards is becoming harder to do as well. All the most popular cards are insanely priced as well due to the limited supply that is left of them. 7900 xtx is a powerhouse of the older generation, but if you're lucky you'll find it for the same price as a 5070 ti.

None of this takes into account the monopoly Nvidia has for local AI workloads. If you want to do local AI, you kind of have to go with Nvidia or work through a lot of hoops with AMD. 

I know Gamer Nexus has a beef with Nvidia currently, (and rightfully so) but I wonder if the current state of the GPU market would shift anything in this video if it was made today.

comments.text: NVIDIA’s recent shift towards a business-driven approach, prioritizing profits over true innovation, mirrors Intel’s own struggles in the semiconductor industry. Both companies have faced issues with innovation stagnation while focusing more on short-term business strategies. Intel, for example, has been struggling to catch up with AMD’s competitive Ryzen chips and has faced delays in its own 7nm process and other technological advancements. Much like NVIDIA's price hikes and artificial product segmentation, Intel has been guilty of releasing incremental updates without truly advancing its core architecture, resulting in a stagnation in performance. While Intel has focused on chasing market share and increasing profit margins, the lack of genuine breakthroughs has left them vulnerable to competitors. NVIDIA's push for AI dominance and Intel’s focus on maintaining a stronghold in the CPU market at all costs both demonstrate a shift away from the original goal of continuous technological progress, leading to frustrated consumers and the eventual rise of alternative companies like AMD and Apple Silicon. Both companies, in their pursuit of profits, have neglected the importance of true innovation, setting themselves up for long-term struggles in an increasingly competitive tech landscape. comments.text:
Just wanted to say that I really appreciate you guys using the FFXIV benchmark as one of your regular tests. To those not aware, that game is heavily CPU-bottlenecked in cases where there are many other player characters on-screen at once. It's a consequence of being built off the old FFXIV 1.0 engine, which itself has its roots in the two-decade-old FFXI engine, which was incredibly CPU-dependent and was targeted primarily to be playable on the PS2.

Better GPUs absolutely improve the performance of that game, but there are still instances where the game will chug if your CPU isn't up to snuff, usually during larger raids and world events such as FATEs and hunts. My trusty old GTX 970 would still regularly break 50fps at 1080p in cutscenes and smaller dungeons/raids, but then drop to under 20fps in populated areas.

1660 Super still going strong. 1080p is fine. I dont want to be all "that moron who thinks 30 and sub 30 fps is no different than 60/120/144/240" but 4k to me just isn't worth it. Give me 1080p at 144 or higher and I'm extremely happy.

Before I even knew what FPS was I always thought it looked "futuristic" over bigger resolution and texture quality. Its exactly the reason why I loved Gran Turismo 1's HD race that took like 4 minutes to load and games like Tekken 3 that ran at a rock solid 60 fps.

To me, especially in Australia there is zero point in buying even a 30 series card because AAA gaming on PC sucks, but it also just sucks extremely heavily in general. They're all the same third person or first person actual crap with zero invovations in gameplay. All the esports titles still run perfectly fine on a 1660 Super.

In the past there would be game releases that made me WANT to upgrade a PC. Quake, UT2k4, Battlefield 2/Oblivion and most recently IIRC I only upgraded to run things like RyuJinx at a decent rate.

There's a severe lack of interesting games that need top end PC hardware that are best played on PC. Most new AAA stuff is either better played on console with a controller and far better load times (GTA5's load times were egregious) and also come with none of the jank that always seems to happen with PC ports (giving up performance to DRM or just piss poor ports).

When I'm forced to upgrade (likely due to something failing at this point), the price to performance ratio will probably still sit me somewhere around a 30 series - if I do it later this year. But I wouldn't even need that for my use cases because PC gaming just isn't needing insane hardware for most games these days.

Those are over a decade old, so that is pretty long ago for technology.  And it certainly  was a heck of a lot of money for a GPU back then.   Most things have increased about 35% since then, independently of demand.  It launched for $329 USD and had the same target as the 5070.  That's the equivalent of about $445 today.  Given the ridiculous increase in demand from the AI sector $549 isn't all that out of line.  The GTX 980 was $549 when it came out, that's around $740.  The 980ti in today's dollars was $877.  Of course, they didn't have close to an equivalent of the xx90 series back then, so think of those as the 5070, 5070ti, and 5080.  Those prices are between $19 and $120 of the MSRP of the current 50 series, and  given the insane demand in the sector, the prices aren't as ridiculous as they seem.  I think NVIDIA could have went even higher without issue.

I think we computer enthusiasts got used to being isolated in our niche that was insulated from other tech sectors.  Bitcoin screwed it up, followed by AI.

comments.text:
Around the acoustics testing - as someone that used to do some work in a similar area (the noise produced by the fans on Commercial Planes), the spikes in the SPL vs frequency charts aren't always important! The tl; dr - some of those spikes may not be very noticeable to the human ear, so shouldn't be the most important thing to point out.

If you see a spike in the SPL vs Frequency graph, what you're getting is a "Tone" or a harmonic of a Tone. These aren't always "annoying" to humans, but are usually considered to more annoying than a broadband with no obvious tones. They are also much more annoying if their harmonics (spikes with 2x or 3x etc. of the same frequency) are in the noise! The larger plot is called a "Broadband" and is often easier to ignore if it is stable - it is a human tendency to ignore noise that doesn't change often - but broadbands are more damaging to your hearing! A lot of acoustic engineering is done to normalise tones out into a broadband (to be less annoying) while reducing the total energy of sound (which is related to the total area under the line). 

Anyway, if you want to use this stuff seriously, I suggest you look into things like dB(A), db(C), and other weighted measurements designed to "interpret" the noise relative to human response. Those measurements will give a weighted measurement on how much a human would care about the fan noise! :)

comments.text:
I don't think I agree with this review's conclusion that this card is representative of "stagnation". ~12% on average generational uplift isn't huge, but it's still a reasonable improvement. Stagnation is what Intel has been doing every release after the 13th gen CPUs; practically no improvement and even some backsliding. At the end of the day, this is a modest improvement over the 4070 Ti Super at a minor price reduction, and it's also matching the 4080 Super at 75% of the price.... At MSRP of course. It would be a fine release... At MSRP.

I think we also have to consider that basically every chip designer has been "stagnating" by the standards described in this video. And I think it's pretty obvious why. The manufacturing processes aren't improving. Getting a ~12% performance improvement while staying on the same TSMC 4N node is genuinely impressive. If the entire industry is blocked on the same manufacturing processes that are out of their control, then A) that's a TSMC / Samsung / Intel problem, and B) that means nvidia's progress is competitive, not stagnating.

Really don't like calling this release "stagnation". I think it shows a lack of care for the context in terms of generations, competition, and engineering.

comments.text: Please work on benchmarks for creators. I could use a new card and frankly it doesn't have to be the best card. It just has to work but I'm not paying these prices. Fingers crossed for the Intel 24GB B60 workstation card. I play very few games per week and war thunder doesn't even need these giant cards with giant prices to work. My experience dates back 35 years and one of the things that's not really covered is what level card creators can get away with if they want to wait a couple minutes to render effects. Back in 1997 I had to render 13 hours for 100 layers of 720x512 resolution. There's a true lack of patience these days with people thinking they need to fastest and best cards, but they do not need this as content creators. If I was cutting a show for broadcast, then my budget would include a pair of rtx6000's and I'd probably be using an overpriced mac pro. However, I'm just getting back into content creation and even a used card from a previous generation will be good enough. I think it's time for people to start thinking about what's good enough vs the best, newest and most expensive option. My experience includes working on the very first HDTV standard with Phillips and Sarnoff while I was still in college. The future is going to be integrated memory like the M2 chip runs but also something like CXL IP that will allow people to add more vram that's addressable. If Intel pushes for integrated memory with their APU's, then there will also be virtual VRAM and it will improve communication between cpu and gpu in the apu but it would in theory allow a gpu in a slot to communicate seamlessly with the processor on the motherboard. As I said, I'm just getting back into things, which includes networking in my own stomping grounds to see where technology is heading. FYI, the full scope of what was being developed 28 to 30 years ago hasn't been fully developed due to technological limitations but now with AI, it's going to give us the power to make a broadcast interactive in the way we envisioned back in the late 90s. Love your channel, Steve, because there's no hype, just facts.

comments.text: Steve, I know you're still newer to sound stuff (relatively speaking here), not sure if you're aware but on the sound charts, the SPL range is far too compressed for the data to be easily readable. You need to either double the resolution the chart displays, or add more graduation lines to the chart so it's easier to follow. 25dB is a MASSIVE range, and while I recognize that the frequency spread falls within that range, representing it at that scale makes it hard to actually see meaningful differences in the 3-6db range when looking frequency. Not a huge gripe since the charts are still technically readable, I just feel like I need to blow the chart up on a 55" TV rather than my 27" monitor, to be able to see the data properly. Maybe I'm overthinking it as an audio nerd, but we always make sure to show things in increments of 6 or 12db so that it's easier to follow how many orders of magnitude something is either louder or quieter at a given frequency. You only use increments of 5-10dB when showing human perceived loudness, not absolute energy values, as a 6db increase is an absolute doubling in energy, but not necessarily a perceived doubling in loudness, because hearing is subjective and weird like that. I understand you want to work with this stuff and show something meaningful, so I'm letting you know this badly needs improvement. In its current state those charts are hot garbage, and you should really replace them or edit them out if you're going to half-ass them that badly

comments.text:
Frame generation is a "win more" technology. If you're already sitting at 60fps (or more), then a bunch of AI generated frames can smooth out your experience - but your experience was already good in the first place. If, on the other hand, you're sitting at 30fps, AI generated frames are just going to look and feel bad. So the ideal use case for this technology is, in fact, the worst use case. The only people who truly benefit form frame gen are those who already have enough frames.

Remember when Nvidia shoved RT cores into budget 20XX series cards like the 2060? That card had no business even attempting ray tracing, but they certainly did charge you a hefty premium for tech you couldn't even use. For most users, ray tracing still isn't worth the 20-40% performance loss outside of the very highest GPU tiers. And while you might expect natural generational uplift to eventually make RT worth it for the masses, we have instead found ourselves in a reality where developers are cashing out all of our performance gains on nonexistent optimization.

The industry is in a very, very bad state.

comments.text:
I've only bought Radeon/AMD as well, but I certainly don't think choosing NVIDIA is the reason for the lack of competition.  That's 100% on AMD and Intel for not coming up with a competitive option for CUDA.  If you are 100% gaming only, I get it.  Stick with AMD every time. But if you do any type of editing it's not even in the same ballpark.  The parallel processing speeds everything up greatly.

Where we are at now is because of two things.  First,  NVIDIA doing some great R&D and striking gold with the CUDA API.  Not to say some luck wasn't involved there, it was originally designed for scientific uses as the parallelization can crunch numbers at insane rates.  They probably saw the potential future of AI, but certainly couldn't have predicted the boom we are seeing.  Their chips just happen to be perfect for the need right now, right place right time and all that.  Second, the competition never really tried.  Intel finally has a GPU that's great for it's cost, but it took them years as they had a hard time seeing past x86.  AMD bought ATI of course and things were good for a while, but once they came up with Zen they've focused on their CPUs and have been taking it to Intel.  Neither of them recognized the competition that NVIDIA was going to be until it was too late.

I really don't have much hope for AMD, I think they will continue to focus on the CPU sector with GPU's being an afterthought.  But Intel may be a different story. XeSS is damn impressive for how new it is, and the upcoming Falcon Shores GPUs could provide some competition with NVIDIA if they are up to snuff.

comments.text:
Four things that I feel need to be pointed out.

1. Intel will see a void in the market and they will get there, it may not be this year, it may not be next but they will. They may not beat Nvidia in raw performance, but if they can get 80-90% of the way there while maintaining sensible pricing, Nvidia will quickly see their market share erode, however its unlikely Nvidia will care because they they’re raking in money with their AI processors.

2. I don’t think Nvidia even gives a shit about the PC community at this point based on their actions in the last year and beyond.

3. If you’re on an older generation and you feel the need to upgrade, you’re going to open your wallet regardless of the price if you can afford it. If your in a position of accumulating debt to pay for a $1000, 1500, or even $2500 GPU, DON’T. Honestly even without the overpricing of 30-40% they’re still expensive and you should probably just buy a console and not sweat putting food on your table, and you won’t be disappointed, consoles are still relatively good value.

4. Don’t buy from an opportunistic scalper, if you do your part of the inflation problem. You can wait a while longer for stock to return to “normal” and buy one from a reputable retailer that isn’t gouging its customers, they exist… at least in Canada they do.

EDIT
All these GPU’s have gotten so fast, and reviewers have become accustomed to frame rates over 100 fps that it’s not hard to get underwhelmed when you look at charts and graphs. It wasn’t long ago that people would jump with joy when they could achieve 70+ frames on 1440p, maybe people need a reality check. PC’s have gotten really really fast. They have reached their peak at this point and unless there’s some new breakthrough technology that will massively decrease node size there’s no reason why anything you buy today will still be good in 3-5 years from now if your looking at the 5080 or 5090 series. The upgrade cycle is elongated, so you pay more now but hardware will age better as they can’t progress as fast. If you’re rocking a 40 series or even a 3090, you probably don’t need to upgrade anyway, if your on a 20 series or older it’s the right time to upgrade (as long as it won’t put you in the poor house.)

comments.text:
Hi Steve, I'm sure you're busy so I don't expect a response, but I think this review lacks a bit of historical perspective.  Whether this is a decent buy depends heavily on what card you're currently using, and whether you're willing to be patient to let supply issues sort themselves out (hopefully), and what you typically expect from a GPU upgrade for this price range.    

While it's certainly not as cheap as I'd like (what ever is?), objectively this card isn't drastically different from previous upgrades I've done in real price or performance.    If you bought a GTX 780 Ti at launch in 2013 like I did, it was a top performing 1080p card at $699.  If you upgraded to a RTX 2080 from that card it was $699.  According to your own 780 Ti revisit video from 5 years ago and some quick napkin math, the performance uplift at 1080p was 170% averaged over 5 games.  Note: I had to use external sources for The Sniper Elite 4 benchmark since you only provided 4k bench in your video, but a performance uplift of 147% in SE4 is in line with other results, certainly good enough for a rough average.

For an upgrade from a 2080 to a 5070 Ti, according to my quick napkin math and your charts, I can expect an average performance uplift of 160% at 4k (without considering DLSS/frame gen)

Adjusted for inflation, the $699 I bought my 2080 for in late 2018 is equivalent to $880 in today's money.  Given the the MSRP price of $750 (equal to ~$600 in 2019 dollars), if I can buy a 5070 Ti for that (through patience or luck) it's actually a deal compared to my last upgrade.  And if I can get it for lets say $850 (which doesn't seem that far fetched, if not tomorrow then probably in a few weeks), I'm spending essentially the same price as I did ~6 years ago for about the same performance uplift (only this time at 4k instead of 1080p).

Viewed through this lens, I don't think it's the absurd, awful, terrible deal you're saying it is.  It's not really Nvidia's fault that inflation spiked between 2019-2025.
